```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.align = "center")
set.seed(2026)
```

## 1. Summary

Six participants performed barbell lifts correctly (class **A**) and incorrectly in four
specific ways (classes **B-E**) while wearing accelerometers on the belt, forearm, arm and
dumbbell (Velloso et al., 2013). The task is to predict the `classe` label from the sensor
readings.

My approach in brief:

1. Remove identifier, timestamp and mostly-empty columns, leaving only sensor measurements.
2. Hold out 30% of the labelled data as a **validation set** that is never used for training or tuning.
3. Train a **random forest** using **5-fold cross-validation** on the remaining 70%.
4. Estimate the out-of-sample error from both the CV result and the untouched validation set.
5. Predict the 20 quiz test cases with the final model.

```{r libs}
library(caret)
library(randomForest)
library(ggplot2)
```

## 2. Data

```{r data}
train_url <- "https://d396qusza40orc.cloudfront.net/predmachlearn/pml-training.csv"
test_url  <- "https://d396qusza40orc.cloudfront.net/predmachlearn/pml-testing.csv"

# Cache local copies so the report can be re-knitted offline
if (!file.exists("pml-training.csv")) download.file(train_url, "pml-training.csv", mode = "wb")
if (!file.exists("pml-testing.csv"))  download.file(test_url,  "pml-testing.csv",  mode = "wb")

na_codes <- c("NA", "", "#DIV/0!")
training <- read.csv("pml-training.csv", na.strings = na_codes)
testing  <- read.csv("pml-testing.csv",  na.strings = na_codes)

dim(training)
dim(testing)
```

## 3. Cleaning and feature selection

The raw file contains many summary-statistic columns (e.g. `kurtosis_*`, `skewness_*`,
`max_*`, `min_*`, `avg_*`, `var_*`, `stddev_*`) that are only filled on the rows where a
new time window begins. They are almost entirely `NA`, and they are also empty in the 20
test cases, so they cannot help prediction there.

I made three choices:

* **Drop columns that are >90% `NA`.** They carry almost no information and cannot be used on the test cases.
* **Drop row index, user name, timestamps and window markers** (`X`, `user_name`,
  `raw_timestamp_part_1/2`, `cvtd_timestamp`, `new_window`, `num_window`). The training
  data are ordered by class and time, so these columns would let a model "predict" `classe` by
  position or time rather than by movement. That would give a deceptively good CV score and
  would not reflect real generalisation.
* **Drop near-zero-variance predictors.**

```{r clean}
na_frac  <- colMeans(is.na(training))
keep     <- names(na_frac)[na_frac <= 0.90]

id_cols  <- c("X", "user_name", "raw_timestamp_part_1", "raw_timestamp_part_2",
              "cvtd_timestamp", "new_window", "num_window")
keep     <- setdiff(keep, id_cols)

training <- training[, keep]
training$classe <- factor(training$classe)

nzv      <- nearZeroVar(training[, setdiff(names(training), "classe")])
if (length(nzv) > 0) training <- training[, -nzv]

predictors <- setdiff(names(training), "classe")
cat("Predictors retained:", length(predictors), "\n")
cat("Any NA remaining in training:", anyNA(training), "\n")
```

The test set is reduced to exactly the same predictor columns (it has no `classe`).

```{r clean-test}
testing_clean <- testing[, predictors]
cat("Any NA remaining in test set:", anyNA(testing_clean), "\n")
```

### Class balance

```{r fig-classes, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.5}
ggplot(training, aes(classe, fill = classe)) +
  geom_bar(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Training observations per class", x = "classe", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Class A (correct execution) is the most common, but the five classes are reasonably
balanced, so plain accuracy is a sensible metric and no resampling for imbalance is needed.

## 4. Model building

### Validation split

I split the labelled data 70/30, stratified on `classe`. The 30% validation set is used
**once**, after the model is final, to get an unbiased out-of-sample estimate.

```{r split}
in_train <- createDataPartition(training$classe, p = 0.70, list = FALSE)
build    <- training[in_train, ]
valid    <- training[-in_train, ]
c(build = nrow(build), validation = nrow(valid))
```

### Cross-validation and model choice

I used **5-fold cross-validation** inside `caret::train()` on the build set. Five folds
balance bias and variance of the error estimate against run time (10 folds is slightly less biased
but about twice as slow on a dataset of this size).

I chose a **random forest** because:

* the predictors are numerous, correlated and on different scales, and random forests need no scaling;
* the relationship between sensor readings and movement error is strongly non-linear, with interactions between sensors;
* forests are robust to noisy features and give built-in variable importance;
* in the original study (Velloso et al.) random forests also performed very well on this data.

```{r train, cache=TRUE}
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 5, allowParallel = TRUE)

rf_fit <- train(classe ~ ., data = build,
                method    = "rf",
                trControl = ctrl,
                tuneLength = 3,
                ntree     = 200)

rf_fit
```

`caret` tuned `mtry` (the number of variables tried at each split) by cross-validated
accuracy and refit on the full build set with the best value.

```{r cv-error}
cv_acc <- max(rf_fit$results$Accuracy)
cat(sprintf("Cross-validated accuracy: %.4f  ->  CV error estimate: %.4f\n",
            cv_acc, 1 - cv_acc))
```

## 5. Out-of-sample error

The cross-validation figure above is already an out-of-sample estimate, since each fold is
predicted by a model that did not see it. It is slightly optimistic, though, because the same
folds were used to choose `mtry`. The held-out validation set has not influenced any
modelling decision and gives the cleaner check.

```{r validate}
pred_valid <- predict(rf_fit, newdata = valid)
cm <- confusionMatrix(pred_valid, valid$classe)
cm$overall[c("Accuracy", "AccuracyLower", "AccuracyUpper")]

oos_error <- 1 - unname(cm$overall["Accuracy"])
cat(sprintf("Validation-set error (expected out-of-sample error): %.4f (%.2f%%)\n",
            oos_error, 100 * oos_error))
```

```{r fig-cm, fig.width=6, fig.height=4.5}
cm_df <- as.data.frame(cm$table)
ggplot(cm_df, aes(Reference, Prediction, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = Freq), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Validation-set confusion matrix") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Expected out-of-sample error.** I take the validation-set error as my best estimate of
the error on new data, and I expect the CV estimate to be close to it. Both are computed in
the chunks above, so the exact figures appear in the knitted output rather than being
hard-coded here.

Two caveats matter for how far to trust this number:

* The 6 participants appear in both the build and validation sets, because the split is random over rows. The estimate therefore measures
  generalisation to **new repetitions by known people**. Accuracy on a completely new
  person would probably be lower. A leave-one-participant-out scheme would measure that,
  but the 20 quiz cases come from the same six people, so row-wise CV matches the actual
  prediction task.
* The validation set is finite, so the estimate has sampling noise. The 95% interval
  printed above (`AccuracyLower`, `AccuracyUpper`) shows its size.

## 6. Which sensors matter?

```{r fig-imp, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=5}
imp <- varImp(rf_fit)$importance
imp$variable <- rownames(imp)
imp <- head(imp[order(-imp$Overall), ], 15)

ggplot(imp, aes(reorder(variable, Overall), Overall)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Top 15 variables by importance", x = NULL, y = "Importance (scaled)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## 7. Final model and the 20 test cases

Having confirmed the approach on held-out data, I refit the same configuration on **all**
labelled rows (build + validation) so the final model uses every available observation, then
predict the 20 test cases.

```{r final}
final_fit <- train(classe ~ ., data = training,
                   method     = "rf",
                   trControl  = trainControl(method = "none"),
                   tuneGrid   = data.frame(mtry = rf_fit$bestTune$mtry),
                   ntree      = 200)

test_pred <- predict(final_fit, newdata = testing_clean)
data.frame(problem_id = testing$problem_id, prediction = test_pred)
```

```{r write-answers}
# One file per problem, in the format used by the course submission page
dir.create("answers", showWarnings = FALSE)
for (i in seq_along(test_pred)) {
  writeLines(as.character(test_pred[i]),
             file.path("answers", paste0("problem_id_", i, ".txt")))
}
```

## 8. Conclusions

* Removing identifier and time columns is essential, because otherwise the model can cheat by position.
* A random forest with 5-fold CV on about 50 sensor predictors separates the five execution styles very accurately.
* The validation-set error reported in Section 5 is my expected out-of-sample error, with the participant caveat noted there.
